mcqs.question: Why doesn't hardware need a separate subtractor circuit alongside the adder?
options: Subtraction is rare enough in real programs to skip optimizing it
a - b is computed as a + (two's-complement negation of b), so the same adder handles both
Subtraction is done entirely in software, not hardware
CPUs use a lookup table for all subtraction results
mcqs.explanation: Two's complement makes negation cheap (invert + add 1), so subtraction reduces to addition with one input inverted and a +1 fed into the carry-in — reusing the same adder circuit.

mcqs.question: What is the hardware rule for detecting signed overflow in an addition?
options: Overflow occurs whenever the final carry-out of the whole adder is 1
Overflow occurs when the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out of the sign bit
Overflow occurs whenever both operands are negative
Overflow occurs whenever the result is larger than 127 in any width
mcqs.explanation: Signed overflow is specifically carry-in XOR carry-out at the sign-bit position — not the overall carry-out (that's the unsigned/carry flag instead), and not simply 'both operands negative' (positive+positive overflow is equally possible and follows the same rule).

mcqs.question: Can the same binary addition set the carry flag but NOT the overflow flag?
options: No, they always agree since both come from the same addition
Yes — they measure different things (unsigned vs signed overflow) and can disagree depending on the operand values
No, carry flag is only used for subtraction
Yes, but only when adding zero
mcqs.explanation: Carry flag reflects unsigned overflow (carry past the top bit); overflow flag reflects signed overflow (carry-in vs carry-out of the sign bit differing). The same bit-level addition can trip one, both, or neither, since they answer different interpretive questions about the same bits.

mcqs.question: In C, why is `if (x + 1 < x)` an unreliable way to check for signed integer overflow?
options: The syntax is invalid in standard C
Signed overflow is undefined behavior, so an optimizing compiler may assume it never happens and remove the check entirely
Integer comparison operators don't work correctly with the + operator
It only works for unsigned integers, and this is a signed comparison
mcqs.explanation: Because signed overflow is UB in C/C++, compilers are allowed to assume x+1 is always greater than x for a signed x, and can optimize the entire check away — a well-known source of security bugs from 'overflow checks' that silently vanish.
